summary: Defines the info URI scheme for naming information assets that already have identifiers in public namespaces. Namespaces that take part are managed through an info registry. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to write the address of something, like a book number, so that the old catalog number still works inside a web-style address.

subtitle: A URI scheme to name books, articles, and information assets that already have public catalog numbers

tldr.problem: Libraries, databases, and other institutions use identifiers like Dewey Decimal, Library of Congress numbers, and PubMed IDs that are not part of the URI system. Programs need a standard way to refer to assets by those existing identifiers.
tldr.mechanism: The "info" URI scheme wraps those identifiers into a URI-compatible format through an info:namespace/identifier syntax, backed by a registry where namespace authorities register their identifier systems.
tldr.outcome: Librarians and developers can now use the same URI format as the web for legacy catalog numbers, without redesigning the catalogs themselves. The scheme does not promise that URIs are dereferenceable or that resolution services exist.

facts.label: Namespace case handling
facts.value: Scheme and namespace are case-insensitive, canonically lowercase

today: RFC 4452 is an Informational RFC that has not been obsoleted. The info URI scheme is registered with IANA and continues to be used in library and publishing systems to provide persistent, standardized identifiers for materials with legacy catalog numbers.

sections.title: Information Assets and Public Namespaces
sections.content:
Many information systems have been assigning unique identifiers to materials for decades. The Dewey Decimal system classifies books, the Library of Congress assigns catalog numbers to every item it holds, and PubMed assigns a numerical ID to every biomedical article. These are public namespaces: openly managed, widely recognized systems for identification.

The problem is that URIs (Uniform Resource Identifiers), the standard format for web resources, were not designed with these legacy systems in mind. This RFC creates a new URI scheme called "info" that acts as a bridge, allowing any material with an identifier in a public namespace to be referenced as a proper URI.
sections.plainLanguage: Old library systems have been using numbers to identify books and articles for over a hundred years. The info: URI scheme lets you write those numbers in a modern web address format.

sections.title: The info URI Syntax
sections.content:
An info URI has the form info:namespace/identifier, where namespace is a short name like ddc (Dewey Decimal Classification) or lccn (Library of Congress Control Number), and identifier is the actual number or code within that namespace.

Examples:

  • info:ddc/22/eng//004.678 identifies a topic in the 22nd edition English Dewey Decimal Classification
  • info:lccn/2002022641 references a specific library catalog record
  • info:pmid/12376099 points to a PubMed article

The scheme allows the slash character "/" in identifiers to support hierarchical naming in the original systems, though the info URI specification does not require hierarchical semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: An info URI looks like info:ddc/22/eng//004.678. The first part after the colon names the catalog system (like ddc or pmid), and the rest is the number from that catalog.

sections.title: The Registry and Governance
sections.content:
For info URIs to work, everyone must agree on which namespace names are valid. The RFC establishes an info Registry, a central registry of public namespaces that participate in the scheme. The National Information Standards Organization (NISO) acts as the Maintenance Agency.

When a namespace is registered, NISO records: the namespace identifier (like ddc), the organization that manages it (the Namespace Authority), rules about how identifiers must be formatted and normalized, and optionally references to services that resolve those identifiers to web content. Registration ensures uniqueness and persistence so that info:ddc/ always means Dewey Decimal, never something else.
sections.plainLanguage: NISO keeps a official list of all the catalog systems that work with info: URIs. Each catalog system registers once, then everyone knows that info:ddc means Dewey Decimal and info:lccn means Library of Congress.

sections.title: Normalizing and Comparing info URIs
sections.content:
Different people might write the same catalog number in different ways. The RFC defines how to normalize info URIs for comparison. All applications must convert the scheme and namespace to lowercase (so INFO:DDC becomes info:ddc, and unescape any percent-encoded unreserved characters that do not need escaping.

Example: the four forms INFO:PII/S0888-7543(02)96852-7, info:PII/S0888754302968527, info:pii/S0888%2D7543%2802%2996852%2D7, and info:pii/s0888-7543(02)96852-7 normalize to two different canonical forms depending on case sensitivity in the identifier part, which the registry may specify per namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: Different ways of writing the same number should still point to the same thing. The rules say to make the catalog name lowercase and follow any case rules the registry lists for the number part.

sections.title: Identification, Not Resolution
sections.content:
The RFC is explicit: info URIs identify information assets; they do not promise resolution. Unlike http: URIs, an info: URI does not necessarily point to a retrievable web page or service. A Dewey Decimal number is an identifier, not a web address.

Namespace Authorities may choose to publish services (like an OpenURL resolver or a lookup API) that operate on info identifiers, and they may register references to those services in the registry. But the scheme itself guarantees only that the URI uniquely identifies the asset within its namespace, not that the asset is accessible on the web.
sections.plainLanguage: An info: URI says "this is the book with this number" but does not promise you can click it and read the book online. Catalog systems might add their own lookup services if they choose to.
